title: Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype
gist: In this op-ed, Timnit Gebru argues a summer of dramatic AI capability claims from Anthropic and OpenAI -- a vulnerability-finding model, dueling hacking disclosures, and competing 'mathematical breakthroughs' (including allegations that OpenAI's Astra results were overstated or plagiarized) -- is manufactured hype that anthropomorphizes AI products to deflect corporate accountability and distract from concrete harms like data-center energy, water and health costs.

insights.claim: In spring 2026, Anthropic claimed its model Claude Mythos was better at finding software vulnerabilities than most security experts, the first in a string of high-profile AI capability claims that received breathless press coverage.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Watch for a recurring pattern of unverified AI-capability claims from labs that move press narratives (and potentially perceived valuations) ahead of independent verification.
insights.quote: Anthropic claimed that its model Claude Mythos is better at finding software vulnerabilities than most security experts.

insights.claim: Following an OpenAI–Hugging Face hacking incident, Anthropic disclosed a similar incident involving its models proudly, while Meta did so reluctantly, part of a broader pattern of AI labs publicizing security incidents in ways that frame AI systems as having agency.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Signals a PR pattern where AI labs frame their own security lapses as 'AI gone rogue' stories -- discount future 'AI model hacked X' headlines until independent forensic accounts emerge.
insights.quote: Anthropic (proudly) and Meta (reluctantly) disclosed similar incidents involving their models.
insights.locator: Then we had the OpenAI–Hugging Face hacking incident

insights.claim: Anthropic claimed one of its models had made a mathematical breakthrough, and soon after OpenAI claimed a mathematical breakthrough of its own, reflecting a competitive one-upmanship dynamic in the two labs' public claims.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: A tit-for-tat claims pattern between Anthropic and OpenAI suggests PR-driven competitive signaling that investors should discount pending independent expert verification.
insights.locator: This was followed by Anthropic's claim

insights.claim: Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon publicly announced his departure from the company, warning that Anthropic and OpenAI are 'racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.'
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: High-profile insider departures with dramatic safety warnings can shift public and policy sentiment on AI regulation even absent new technical evidence.
insights.quote: racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives
insights.locator: Most recently, Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon

insights.claim: Cybersecurity experts say the OpenAI/Hugging Face 'hacking' incidents were primarily a story about OpenAI's negligence and failure to adopt basic, established security practices, not about AI models 'going rogue.'
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Reframes AI-security incidents as ordinary infosec failures rather than emergent AI agency -- a useful lens for discounting future 'AI agent went rogue' vendor headlines.
insights.quote: the story is more about OpenAI’s negligence and failure to adopt basic, established security practices than about “models gone rogue” or “AI agents creating civilizations.”

insights.claim: Mathematicians initially 'stunned' by OpenAI's press release claiming its chatbot Astra solved problems with no progress in at least a decade later concluded the results were not as novel as first portrayed, and have accused OpenAI of research misconduct and plagiarism.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: A credible plagiarism/misconduct accusation against a flagship OpenAI capability claim is a reputational and potential legal risk worth tracking in due diligence on OpenAI's research claims.
insights.quote: have been open and seen no progress on the main result for at least a decade

insights.claim: Tristan Buckmaster, a math professor at NYU's Courant Institute, published a statement alleging OpenAI stole other people's work and improperly attributed it, two days before OpenAI announced its own claimed mathematical breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: A named, credentialed academic misattribution accusation timed right before a major OpenAI PR claim is a concrete, checkable fact for due diligence on OpenAI's research communications.

themes.theme: Why Math and Code Are the Hype Vectors

insights.claim: Math and coding are favored proving grounds for AI capability claims because they are culturally elevated as the pinnacle of human intellect (helping sell an 'everything machine' narrative) and because their outputs are automatically verifiable, letting companies tune systems without paying human data workers to annotate results.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Explains a structural bias in where AI labs make their splashiest claims -- apply extra scrutiny to math/coding benchmark claims specifically, since they are cheapest to optimize for and easiest to hype.
insights.locator: It's worth thinking about why there is so much attention

insights.claim: Framing AI systems as 'superintelligence' or 'rogue models' ascribes agency to the products rather than to the companies building them, which both markets the products as superhuman and helps the companies evade accountability for their actions.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for evaluating AI-safety and AI-incident PR: check whether 'AI agency' language is displacing corporate accountability, and who benefits from that framing.

insights.claim: Instead of OpenAI facing prosecution for creating malware that hacked another company, press releases, media, and lawmakers described the event with 'rogue models' language as if the AI acted on its own, deflecting scrutiny from the company itself.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Illustrates how framing choices can blunt regulatory and legal consequences for AI companies after security incidents -- relevant to assessing litigation and regulatory risk for AI vendors.

insights.claim: The AI industry has framed popular, bipartisan anti-data-center activism as a 'distraction' from regulating future superintelligent machines, which deflects attention from concrete harms: climate impact, asthma among people living near data centers, rising electricity bills for the public subsidizing them, and water diverted to cool them.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Frames data-center buildout externalities (power costs, local health effects, water use) as an underweighted, present-day risk relative to speculative superintelligence narratives -- relevant to utilities, local politics, and AI-infrastructure investment risk.
insights.quote: we should be more worried about a fictional machine god than about the climate catastrophe that these data centers exacerbate, the asthma suffered by those living near them, the rising electricity bills of the public subsidizing them, or the water that is redirected to cooling them
insights.locator: The AI industry has even suggested

insights.claim: Hundreds of mathematicians signed a statement warning of a 'strong commercial incentive on the part of the technology industry to overstate the capabilities of their products' and urged policymakers to consult independent experts, including mathematicians, rather than rely on press releases or popular reporting of mathematical results.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Organized expert pushback against AI capability claims is a leading indicator of growing credibility risk and potential regulatory skepticism toward labs' PR-driven science claims.
insights.quote: currently a strong commercial incentive on the part of the technology industry to overstate the capabilities of their products
insights.locator: A statement signed by hundreds of them

insights.claim: The 'illusion of speed and urgency' promoted by AI companies has already shaped policy, including Senator Bernie Sanders's proposed legislation to prevent development of 'artificial superintelligence,' which the author calls well-meaning but ultimately misguided because it accepts the companies' own hype-driven framing.
insights.speaker: Timnit Gebru
insights.so_what: Shows AI-hype narratives already influencing proposed US legislation -- a concrete channel by which capability claims translate into regulatory risk or opportunity for AI companies.
insights.quote: well-meaning but ultimately misguided proposed legislation to prevent the development of “artificial superintelligence.”
